papers.title: Tracing Knowledge and Reasoning in LLM
papers.authors: Yang Wang, Xiao Wang, Yiqi Liu, Chenghao Xiao, Eleni Vasilaki, Goran Nenadic, Chenghua Lin
papers.abstract: Current evaluations of Large Language Models (LLMs) report performance at the dataset or task level, revealing what a model achieves but offering little insight into the internal processing associated with its performance. We propose a task-centric framework for characterising the model-internal processing elicited by a benchmark. It combines attention- and activation-based signals with representation-based measures to characterise benchmarks spanning a continuum from retrieval-dominant to reasoning-dominant and to surface failure modes that task-level scores conceal. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks and conduct targeted internal-state analyses on representative models and tasks, observing systematic differences in processing between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks. We shift evaluation from asking what score a model achieves toward characterising the processing patterns associated with that score, potentially supporting more targeted benchmark selection and more informed model choice. We open source our code at https://github.com/extraordinarylab/trace-kr.

papers.title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
papers.abstract: Scaling quantum computing toward practical quantum advantage is currently limited by the efficiency of circuits that operate on information encoded by quantum error-correcting codes. The full stack of quantum computing encompasses several tasks: preparation of logical code states, implementation of logical gates, logical routines on encoded qubits, etc. Yet, these circuits are largely designed by hand for individual cases, with some recent works incorporating machine learning for certain aspects. We formulate this problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, wherein a large language model, leveraging its pretraining knowledge and tool-use proficiency, and guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for a wide range of curated tasks such as logical state preparation, logical gate design, and logical routines such as code-switching, code growth, etc. Our approach consistently finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of these tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults.

papers.title: Detection and Classification in Latent Spaces: High-Dimensional Analysis and Validation
papers.authors: Enis Chenchene, Anil S. Baslamisli, Paolo Braca
papers.abstract: Foundation models produce high-dimensional latent representations in which suitably designed statistical decision rules can be effective yet analytically tractable. We study such detectors in the high-dimensional regime, where latent dimension and training sample size grow proportionally. For linear and quadratic statistics, we derive explicit large-deviation characterizations of false-alarm and miss-detection performance under the Neyman-Pearson paradigm, and show how the binary analysis extends to multi-class classification. The resulting error probabilities and corresponding decay rates exhibit non-monotonic dependence on the shape parameter, including double-descent and, in some regimes, multiple-descent. Experiments on vision, text, and audio datasets using modern foundation models show close agreement between theoretical predictions and empirical performance. In particular, the proposed framework allows us to set a prescribed false-alarm level and accurately predict the corresponding miss-detection probability. Overall, our results provide a theoretically grounded and interpretable framework with competitive empirical performance across different modalities.

papers.title: Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles
papers.authors: Wang Ma, Debarun Bhattacharjya, Junkyu Lee, Nhan H Pham, Harsha Kokel, Qiang Ji
papers.abstract: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.

papers.title: Unsupervised learning reveals a small number of galaxy formation pathways in IllustrisTNG
papers.authors: C. Alvarez-Fernandez, H. Dominguez Sanchez, J. Vega-Ferrero, E. Angeloudi, A. Ferre-Mateu, D. Sotillo-Ramos
papers.abstract: Understanding the main drivers of galaxy formation and the connection between observable properties and evolutionary pathways is a central goal of extragalactic astronomy. Observations provide single-epoch snapshots of galaxies at different stages of their development, whereas cosmological simulations allow us to trace the full formation histories of individual systems within a theoretical framework. Extracting information from these datasets remains challenging. Our aim is to use machine-learning techniques to unveil physical properties from the simulation datasets. We apply two unsupervised ML techniques, dimensionality reduction and clustering, to identify galaxy evolution key parameters. We use UMAP as our dimensionality reduction tool and k-means as our clustering method. We perform dimensionality reduction on the star formation histories (SFHs) of a sample of aproximately 10000 galaxies drawn from the TNG50 and TNG100 simulations. The resulting representation of the SFHs in a two-dimensional UMAP space reveals a clear ordering of galaxy mass assembly histories, separating quenched and star-forming systems, as well as galaxies with significant ex situ stellar mass contributions. Galaxy properties from simulation catalogs that are not used in the dimensionality reduction show correlations across the UMAP plane. Furthermore, using a k-means clustering analysis, we identify six groups of galaxies with distinct evolutionary histories. These groups show systematic differences in stellar mass, morphology, angular momentum, star formation activity, and merger history, and occupy different regions of the SFR-mass and mass-size planes. Our results indicate that the diversity of galaxy formation histories in IllustrisTNG can be organized into a small number of characteristic evolutionary pathways linking galaxy accretion histories and present-day structural and star-forming properties.
